report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is plausible but overstated. Evidence does **not** establish that simply being vegetarian increases life expectancy compared with eating meat. Most studies measure death rates over follow-up, not actual years of life gained, and they are observational—so differences in smoking, alcohol, exercise, weight, income, and health-conscious behavior may partly explain results.

**Evidence supporting it:** In the large Adventist Health Study-2, vegetarian dietary patterns were associated with lower all-cause mortality than nonvegetarian patterns (about 12% lower after adjustment); the association was clearer in men. This supports a possible longevity benefit, particularly within a population with relatively low smoking and alcohol use.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4191896/

**Evidence against a universal benefit:** In EPIC-Oxford, which compared vegetarians and comparable nonvegetarians in the UK, overall mortality did not materially differ. Thus, the Adventist result has not replicated consistently across populations.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4691673/

An Australian prospective cohort likewise reported that prior studies were limited and inconsistent when assessing self-identified vegetarianism and mortality—an important warning against treating vegetarian status itself as causal.  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s41043-023-00460-9

**What seems better supported:** *Quality* of plant-based eating matters more than the label. In UK Biobank, greater adherence to a **healthful** plant-based pattern was associated with lower mortality, cancer, and especially cardiovascular-disease risk. A vegetarian diet high in refined grains, sugar, or ultra-processed foods would not necessarily confer that advantage; a meat-containing diet rich in plant foods may also be healthy.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2802814
